danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: I de første dage af oktober kom endnu en udsending til Kutuzov med et brev fra Napoleon, hvori han foreslog fred, og som var falsk dateret fra Moskva, skønt Napoleon allerede var ikke langt fra Kutuzov på den gamle Kalugavej. Kutuzov besvarede dette brev, som han havde besvaret det, Lauriston tidligere bragte, med at der ikke kunne være tale om fred.

Kort efter indløb der en rapport fra Dorokhovs guerillaenhed, der opererede til venstre for Tarutino, om at tropper fra Broussiers division var blevet set ved Forminsk, og at de, adskilt fra resten af den franske hær, let kunne tilintetgøres. Soldaterne og officererne forlangte atter handling. Generaler i staben, begejstrede over erindringen om den lette sejr ved Tarutino, opfordrede Kutuzov til at følge Dorokhovs forslag. Kutuzov anså ikke noget offensivt for nødvendigt. Resultatet blev et kompromis, der var uundgåeligt: en lille styrke blev sendt til Forminsk for at angribe Broussier.

Ved et mærkeligt tilfælde blev denne opgave, der viste sig at være yderst vanskelig og vigtig, betroet Dokhturov — den samme beskedne lille Dokhturov, som ingen har beskrevet for os som en, der udkastede slagplaner, galopperede foran regimenter, strøede kors over batterier og så videre, og som blev anset for og omtalt som ubeslutsom og utydelig — men som vi finder i kommando, hvor stillingen var vanskeligst, gennem alle de russisk-franske krige fra Austerlitz til 1813. Ved Austerlitz blev han som den sidste ved Augesddæmningen, samlede regimenterne og reddede, hvad reddes kunne, da alle flygtede og gik til grunde, og der ikke var en eneste general tilbage i bagtroppen. Syg med feber drog han til Smolensk med tyve tusind mand for at forsvare byen mod hele Napoleons hær. Ved Smolensk, ved Malakhov-porten, var han næppe faldet i søvn i et feberanfald, før bombardementet af byen vækkede ham — og Smolensk holdt stand hele dagen. Ved Borodino, da Bagration var faldet, og ni tiendedele af vor venstrefløj var blevet nedmejet, og hele den franske artilleriild var rettet mod den, var den mand, der blev sendt derhen, den samme ubeslutsomme og utydelige Dokhturov — Kutuzov, der skyndte sig at rette en fejl, han havde begået ved først at sende en anden. Og den stille lille Dokhturov red derhen, og Borodino blev den russiske hærs største ære. Mange helte er blevet beskrevet for os i vers og prosa, men om Dokhturov er der knap nok sagt et ord.

Det var atter Dokhturov, de sendte til Forminsk og derfra til Malo-Jaroslavets, stedet hvor det sidste slag med franskmændene blev udkæmpet, og hvor den franske hærs tydelige opløsning begyndte. Og vi fortælles om mange genier og helte i den periode af felttoget, men om Dokhturov siges intet eller meget lidt, og det endda tvivlsomt. Og denne tavshed om Dokhturov er det klareste vidnesbyrd om hans fortjeneste.

Det er naturligt for et menneske, der ikke forstår en maskines virkemåde, at forestille sig, at en spån, der tilfældigt er faldet ned i den og forstyrrer dens gang, er dens vigtigste del. Den, der ikke forstår maskinens konstruktion, kan ikke begribe, at det lille forbindelseshjul, der drejer stille rundt, er en af de mest væsentlige dele, og ikke spånen, der blot skader og hindrer maskinens gang.

Den tiende oktober, da Dokhturov var nået halvvejs til Forminsk og havde gjort holdt i landsbyen Aristovo, trofast i færd med at udføre de ordrer, han havde modtaget, nåede hele den franske hær, i sin krampagtige bevægelse, tilsyneladende frem til Murats position for at give slag — men slog pludselig uden nogen grund ind på den nye Kalugavej og begyndte at rykke ind i Forminsk, hvor kun Broussier havde været indtil da. På det tidspunkt havde Dokhturov under sin kommando foruden Dorokhovs afdeling de to små guerillaenheder under Figner og Seslavin.

Om aftenen den ellevte oktober kom Seslavin til hovedkvarteret i Aristovo med en fransk gardist, han havde taget til fange. Fangen fortalte, at de tropper, der var rykket ind i Forminsk den dag, var hele hærens fortrop, at Napoleon var dér, og at hele hæren havde forladt Moskva fire dage forinden. Samme aften fortalte en livegen fra Borovsk, at han havde set en umådelig hær rykke ind i byen. Nogle kosakker fra Dokhturovs afdeling rapporterede, at de havde set den franske garde marchere ad vejen mod Borovsk. Af alle disse rapporter fremgik det klart, at hvor man havde ventet at møde én division, stod nu hele den franske hær, der marcherede fra Moskva i en uventet retning — ad Kalugavejen. Dokhturov var uvillig til at foretage sig noget, da det ikke stod ham klart, hvad han burde gøre. Han havde fået ordre til at angribe Forminsk. Men dengang havde kun Broussier været dér, og nu var hele den franske hær dér. Jermolov ønskede at handle på eget initiativ, men Dokhturov insisterede på, at han måtte have Kutuzovs instrukser. Så blev det besluttet at sende en depeche til staben.

Til dette formål blev en dygtig officer, Bolkhovitiov, valgt, som ud over at aflevere en skriftlig rapport skulle forklare hele sagen mundtligt. Hen imod midnat galopperede Bolkhovitiov af sted med depechen og mundtlige instrukser til generalstaben, ledsaget af en kosak med reserveheste.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: In the early days of October, another envoy came to Kutuzov with a letter from Napoleon proposing peace, falsely dated from Moscow, though Napoleon was already not far from Kutuzov on the old Kaluga road. Kutuzov replied as he had to Lauriston's earlier letter, saying there could be no question of peace.

Soon after, a report came in from Dorokhov's guerrilla detachment, operating to the left of Tarutino, that troops from Broussier's division had been spotted at Forminsk and, being separated from the main French army, could easily be destroyed. The soldiers and officers again demanded action. Generals on the staff, emboldened by the easy victory at Tarutino, urged Kutuzov to follow Dorokhov's suggestion. Kutuzov didn't think any offensive was necessary. The result was an inevitable compromise: a small detachment was sent to Forminsk to attack Broussier.

By a strange coincidence, this task—which turned out to be one of the most difficult and important of the campaign—was given to Dokhturov, that same modest little Dokhturov whom no one has ever described drawing up battle plans, charging in front of regiments, or showering decorations on batteries, and who was considered and spoken of as indecisive and lacking insight. Yet we find him in command at the most critical position in every engagement of the Russo-French wars from Austerlitz to 1813. At Austerlitz he was the last to hold the Augezd dam, rallying regiments and saving what he could when everyone was fleeing and not a single general remained in the rear guard. Ill with fever, he went to Smolensk with twenty thousand men to defend it against Napoleon's entire army. At the Malakhov Gate in Smolensk, he had barely dozed off in a bout of fever before being woken by the bombardment—and Smolensk held out all day. At Borodino, when Bagration was killed and nine-tenths of the men on the left flank had fallen and the full force of French artillery was directed there, the man sent to that spot was this same 'irresolute and unperceptive' Dokhturov—Kutuzov rushing to correct a mistake he'd made by first sending someone else. And the quiet little Dokhturov rode there, and Borodino became the greatest glory of the Russian army. Many heroes of that time have been celebrated in verse and prose, but about Dokhturov, scarcely a word has been said.

It was Dokhturov again who was sent to Forminsk and from there to Malo-Yaroslavets—the site of the last battle with the French, where the obvious disintegration of the French army began. We hear about many geniuses and heroes of that campaign, but about Dokhturov, nothing or almost nothing, and even that is said doubtfully. This silence about Dokhturov is the clearest proof of his merit.

It's natural for someone who doesn't understand how a machine works to assume that a wood shaving that has accidentally fallen into it and is bouncing around, interfering with its operation, must be its most important part. Someone who doesn't understand the machine's construction can't grasp that the small connecting cog, turning quietly, is one of the most essential parts—not the shaving that merely damages and hinders it.

On October tenth, Dokhturov had gotten halfway to Forminsk and stopped at the village of Aristovo, faithfully preparing to carry out his orders. Then the entire French army—having lurched convulsively toward Murat's position as if to give battle—suddenly and for no apparent reason veered left onto the new Kaluga road and began pouring into Forminsk, where previously only Broussier had been. At that point, Dokhturov had under his command, besides Dorokhov's detachment, the two small guerrilla bands of Figner and Seslavin.

On the evening of October eleventh, Seslavin arrived at Aristovo headquarters with a captured French guardsman. The prisoner said the troops entering Forminsk that day were the vanguard of the entire army—Napoleon was there, and the whole army had left Moscow four days earlier. That same evening, a house servant from Borovsk said he'd seen an enormous army entering the town. Cossacks from Dokhturov's detachment reported sighting the French Guards marching toward Borovsk. From all these reports, it was clear that where they had expected to find a single division, they now faced the entire French army, marching from Moscow in an unexpected direction along the Kaluga road. Dokhturov was unwilling to act, as it was no longer clear what he should do. He'd been ordered to attack Forminsk, but at that time only Broussier had been there—now the whole French army was there. Ermolov wanted to act on his own judgment, but Dokhturov insisted on getting instructions from Kutuzov. So it was decided to send a dispatch to the staff.

For this mission, they chose a capable officer named Bolkhovitinov, who was to explain the situation verbally as well as deliver a written report. Toward midnight, Bolkhovitinov received the dispatch and verbal instructions and galloped off to General Staff headquarters, accompanied by a Cossack with spare horses.
